empty_choir.doctrine: No successor stewards after the casting-out. The First Verse (A.V. 450) is creation's standing stewardship ordinance; the Crown glyph is its anchor and interface; each King's anointment renews its executing authority ('the cycle'). The Twelve Shepherds are its tuners.
empty_choir.modern_crisis: Verse aged 1,875 years; the Eight probe its edges; the A.V. 2325 glyph hesitation was approach to authority-failure; Echo amended the Verse with a new note.

echo_wound.doctrine: Anharas sang incompletely, not falsely; Incarnation means accepting embodied limitation; the Wound is why the Twelve exist

irregular_cycle.doctrine: Early renewal cycles ~250 years; intervals shortening/irregularizing = measurable Verse decay; 2325 hesitation as terminal data point

two_crowns.doctrine: The glyph declares the Verse requires renewed embodied authority — not the King's death. A.V. 2325 is unprecedented: renewal called while Osric lives. Osric = civil King; Echo = metaphysical bearer. A constitutional and theological catastrophe with no statute or precedent.

SANDLINE systems specification and campaign mission manifest added. Two integration defects in the original design document resolved: (1) species-coded resource systems ('Elven Arcane Stress', 'Goblin Volatility') re-keyed to materiel — Arcane Stress follows Veskar cells and Scrap Volatility follows scavenged weapons, in any hands, per TR2/KC2/IA1; (2) the procedural five-layer node graph reconciled with the authored five-act campaign as an authored spine with rotation pools between spine missions. Divergence Ledger specified with doctrinal-play compensation so neither build dominates. Act V horror systems, squad class mapping with bond tracks, and dual supply channels specified. 32-mission manifest across five acts.

ThinShot repository assessed and adopted as the SANDLINE implementation. Mechanical precedence inverted: the shipped Godot build outranks the Sand & Sorcery design document and the GS1 systems specification for mechanics, because its systems are implemented and play-tuned while the specs are not; the Codex retains absolute precedence over fiction, naming, factions, and doctrine. The Goblin Rust Choir framing is struck as a TR2/KC2/IA1 violation and reframed as the Thirst (sprites retained, framing replaced); Desert Scouts become Kestrel Squad. The repo's permadeath-with-garrison-replacement attrition model is adopted as canonical, superseding GS1 SS.7. Annex VIII.2 to be rewritten to describe the actual build (move-once/shoot-once, adjacency cover, magazines and fire modes) rather than the unbuilt AP/D20 spec. Five-phase conversion roadmap issued.

The Cartographer is canonically the surveyor-collector of ThinShot's Operation Second Verse. The repository independently invented an antagonist 'at the end of the tracks' who keeps surveyors alive 'because somebody wanted the maps in their heads'; canon's Riverspoken are led by the Confederacy's former survey-master who mapped the dead watercourses for forty years. These are the same character, and the repo's version is adopted rather than overwritten. Operation Second Verse becomes SANDLINE's on-ramp to Act IV.

Rules.gd is the canonical home of SANDLINE combat arithmetic. Any Grounded Doctrine mechanic expressible as a number belongs there with an assertion in test_rules.gd; the Codex will not respecify in prose what the module states in code. Extends RM1's mechanical precedence from 'the build outranks the spec' to 'the build is the spec'.

Canon integration plan issued for the SANDLINE repository. Governing split reaffirmed: fiction conforms to the Codex, mechanics conform to the build. Hard constraint recorded from the codebase itself — Kind and TEAM_* ordinals are persisted in save files, so renaming may never reorder them; new kinds are appended and the save version climbed. Ruled that goblin identifiers, enum members, and sprite paths are RETAINED: canon governs player-visible text, not developer identifiers, and the Thirst are goblins — the error corrected by IA1/KC2 was the rabble framing, never the species. Faction relabelling is concentrated in the single Unit.kind_role_name() match block. Five phases: rename (no test may change result), Grounded Doctrine (Named Dead, surrender/rout, contacts-resolved scoring, the Notebook on save v3, bystanders reusing prisoner plumbing, Standing and Strain), the six remaining Kestrels, the Strange via the Cartographer, and Old Promise.

Combat doctrine corrected against pacifist-optimum drift. GS1 SS.5's 'fewest names added to the roll' scoring made every kill a point deduction, told the player a clean firefight was a partial failure, and gave them a reason to optimise against grief rather than read the names. Replaced structurally: the military outcome is graded, the human cost is reported, and the two are never summed. Killing armed combatants in honest combat costs nothing; only chosen conduct costs. Restraint is priced (turn, position, prisoner obligation) so it stays a decision. No pacifist run: kill floors, unbreakable enemy classes, and at least one mission where hesitation kills a squadmate and the drill is right. Alliance Strain carries a floor no conduct clears — perfect play earns tolerance, never welcome, because the objection is that Crown hands are killing Confederacy countrymen at all.

Complete canon rewrites authored for all seven shipped missions (Appendix A of the integration plan): fiction, briefing, orders, and debrief for each, with no mechanical field touched. The Charter of Wells becomes the reason for every mission in Operation Dry Well; the Rangers' souring is carried in the text of The Long Haul, where the squad burns a water column in a country that has argued about wells for three centuries. The repo's Crown depot mark and canon's Tarkesh Wound-steel Mattocks are unified rather than chosen between — Crown crates containing factory-new Tarkesh rifles from a foundry unwritten in A.V. 1983 — which merges the shipped mystery with the Act IV hook. The Choirmaster becomes THE SURVEY CAMP and its objective END THE READING; the Cartographer is present by absence, his forty years of survey annotated into a schedule, and he is not among the bodies. Per GS2 no briefing implies the killing was avoidable and no debrief grades the player.

The Quiet Tax adopted as canon and filed in the Scenes volume as a complete short story (A.V. 2324, one year before the glyph hesitates). It uses existing canon correctly and adds to it. New canon ratified: the Raven LISTENER discipline — operatives who measure resonance loss by ear, report attenuation as a percentage, and at the height of the discipline end a working with one correct tone; the Hushfolk cups as ANCHORS rather than mere drains, giving the Quiet War a containment method (break the cups, un-anchor the Almoner); the Almoner's sewn mouth and the thread that snaps; Quietors in ordinary clothes with no weapons; the failure of Veil runecraft under null-adjacent interference and the brick that worked instead, adopted as a fifth design counterweight; the Queen's Garden's operational sandwiches and its creative accounting (sixty-three chimes from storm-water displacement mitigation to house nine people, over Raven objection to the code); the erasure of a constabulary report between 03:17 and 03:41; and the low C of a passing Glassline tram, which every Eclipsera child knows before the national anthem. New figures: Corren Vey, Mara Sen, Aven Draal, Patrolman Edrin Vale.

Rodar Akai origin, temperament, and the hometown thread. Author-supplied ruling adopted; filed as KC4 because the submitted ID (KC2) was already assigned to the Countrymen/Riverspoken ruling. Amends KC1 without replacing it. Rodar's civilian occupation canonized as warehouse hand at the Dray Cross freight yards, which pays off diegetically in Act IV when he reads the Wound-steel crates as a dock hand and recognizes the missing paper trail as the evidence. His induction temperament canonized as a boot who wanted the letter — abrasive in speech, decent in deed, ignorance never cruelty — with the arc running loud boot to quiet contact survivor to reluctant leader, the promotion landing after the shell cracks. Rodar and Brukk Meshan share a hometown but not a street: starting friction rather than starting friendship, with Rodar carrying secondhand interior-town condescension he does not know he holds. New location Dray Cross (name provisional): Crown-interior rail and canal junction with a Tarkesh-diaspora quarter from the post-1980 dispersals — the war does not come there, it takes people from there. New opening mission Last Shift added to the manifest; Brukk's Act II bond mission routed through home. Josen Marr rider ratified: with Rodar he forms the axis of desire without gift against gift without desire.

Inspector Emrys Ashcombe canonized: elf, 214, forty-one years in the Eclipsera Constabulary, conscripted under the Levy because a clerk matched a skill code for first-hand human intelligence, and seconded to the Accord Ranger Program as Field Intelligence Officer attached to Kestrel Squad — attached rather than line, preserving KC1's eight. He is the diegetic source of the Grounded Doctrine's content: Named Dead enrichment, contact rounds, non-violent interrogation that makes accepting surrender practically rather than morally advantageous, and Riverspoken early warning. Design edge ratified: the skill that humanises the enemy is the skill that finds him, and he makes killing informed rather than avoidable (GS2-compliant). Frictions established with Sillae Vekh (belonging versus technique) and with the Confederacy at large, for whom a Crown elf is harder to forgive than a human occupier. Structurally he is Corven Sayle's camouflage — the squad never wonders about the quartermaster because it already has an intelligence officer — and he alone is unsurprised by the Act IV reveal. Carries an unresolved hook: an A.V. 2319 Eclipsera case he closed as ordinary crime that was a Hushfolk working (QT1). Permadeath applies; his loss removes the intelligence layer for the remainder of the campaign.

The Ilyas repository (github.com/bfunkmcgee/ilyas; working title Ragdoll Skirmish Lab) is adopted as a Veil game layer: a turn-based melee RPG in one browser page, in which dice decide each exchange and procedural ragdolls act the result out. Its story is a prologue, The Long Night, set in Eclipsera on one night of A.V. 2321, and Act I, the Pit, whose built scenes cover the six weeks after; beside the story it keeps a skirmish lab of free fights. Its fiction source is the author's Ragdoll Skirmish: Veil Synopsis (2026-10-21), whose table of new material is filed as LN2 to LN11 together with what the build has added since. The RM1/RM6 split governs: fiction, naming, factions and doctrine conform to the Codex; mechanics conform to the build, which outranks any design text for them. Player-visible names carry the synopsis's collision fixes: Kael to Ilyas against Kael Tharanis, Mara to Amri against Mara Sen, Vargo to Qadir, Vosk to Ixet and Varn to Doran against V-name crowding, and Halloran to Hallowell. The code keeps Kael as its own word for the hero, as RM6 kept SANDLINE's identifiers. Recorded as game state [G] in Book VIII.4: the stages and scenes, tempo and balance pips, the arc-blade's stances and lash, the workings and their costs, Aether, Overdrive, levels 1 to 100 and style expertise 1 to 20, the signature weapons, and the finale's choice to spare or behead Auden Hallowell, of which canon keeps the beheading (LN4). Assessed at V95, commit 17f2970.

Ilyas Tehrun is a desert elf, the Sareth family's enforcer for thirty years, who looks early thirties because elves age slowly. Before that he was an Elven Ranger of Noon Company, the only Ranger cohort ever gilded. In A.V. 2274 Ranger armorers went after the weakest part of a battery rifle, a cell that can be dropped, emptied or taken, and made the body the cell: forty volunteers had a V-cell lattice inked into them in drawn gold wire, routed by hand along each one's own nerves, no two patterns alike. It worked, and then it burned. A gilded body has no cell bay to vent, so Mana Burn takes the wearer instead of the weapon, and within three years most of the company had cooked from the inside. The deaths were filed with the Overdrive recalls (VII.4.3) as training accidents and the pattern books sealed in A.V. 2277; nobody has drawn the lattice since. The survivors stayed in service, attached to nothing and watched by everyone, and other Rangers call them lamps, half salute and half pity: a lamp gives light by burning, and it burns out. Ilyas walked out in A.V. 2290, the year the Confederacy passed its statute against selling its edge. He was a piece of that edge, and he sold it to the Sareths: thirty years before the Long Night he drank from their cup. Gold lines run from his wrists to his collar, and where he once pushed too hard a line has burned out to a dull scar. Clarified: all Ranger kit carries arcane gold circuitry (V.5.1), and Noon Company alone carried it in the body. The gilt is Confederacy battery-tech (VII.0) in the nerves. It locks his arc-blade, nine blued plates that unroll from the hilt and lock rigid on a thread of V-cell current, and it powers his workings, of which canon names three: the Gilt bolt, the Gale and the Glimmer step. Aether is the game's word for the gilt's charge, and the game's further workings are game state (LN1). Book VII.0.1.

The Sareth family is a desert-elf syndicate of Confederacy expatriates in the Arclight Sprawl, running the underlevels' smuggling out of the Cistern Quarter. A member swears by drinking from the family's cup, a criminal echo of the Cupbearers' Oath (VIII.3.7). The family owns an old smuggling railway under the Sprawl, the Sareth line, which predates the Glassline on that side of the city and once carried Confederacy goods under the streets. One of its stops lies under the Lantern Bistro on Lamplight Street, reached by a private lift behind a tiled wall in the kitchen. Its last station, the Deep Station, lay where Hallowell later raised his tower, and Hallowell's people hold that end. The family keeps a helicopter, a long memory for what it has bought, and a cleaner who is never named: the man in white. On the roof of Hallowell Tower he gave the family's answer in its own words: the family was never here tonight. Book V.3.1.

Auden Hallowell is the son of Perrin Hallowell, who founded Hallowell Arms in A.V. 2212 (VII.4.4), and old enough to remember the stamping presses, which makes the Hallowells elves. He held one of the family's seats on the Lumen Vast board, theirs since the acquisition of A.V. 2301. In A.V. 2321 he was the man behind the Gutter Dumping trade, pushing warehouse-grade pistols into the underlevels at volume through streets the Sareths consider theirs, and to protect the trade he had bought every Eclipsera Constabulary badge between the Sprawl's farm edge and his tower in the Tower District. On one night that year, from an hour before midnight to just past it, the Sareths sent Ilyas Tehrun for him: through six hired men at the farm edge, three Kindling riders on the avenue, a Constabulary checkpoint, Qadir Mell and the Lantern Bistro, the Line's goblins and their keeper, the tower's lobby, and Hallowell's head of security. Auden Hallowell, who never fought, was beheaded in his office; of the game's two endings canon keeps this one (LN1). Hallowell Arms settled the Gutter Dumping affair without admission after his death, and that is the settlement VII.4.4 records. On the roof the family's man in white put out Ilyas's light with a null-rim round (LN5) and sent him over the edge, because a denial is only as good as its loose ends.

A null-rim round is a single round quenched at a null rim, fired from one pistol of a cased Maben Register Pair (VII.4.5); its voicing climbs as it comes up to charge. It is kin to the Quiet Nail, forged at a null rim (X.6), and to the null zones of the Northern Continuum (V.4). Through a gilded body it takes the null with it: every line of the lattice goes dark, and the null settles in the gilt and stays. The workings fail, the arc-blade becomes nine loose plates that will not lock, any cell wired in near the wearer dies, and the null along his nerves holds him to a man's pace. The Sareths ordered theirs the year Ilyas drank from their cup: thirty years of keeping a way to put out their lamp. Gilt cut away from the body before the null reaches it stays lit, and its light keeps the flesh from turning. Falling into the Pit, Ilyas was caught through the right forearm by a spike on the wall and hung there until his own weight tore the arm out at the shoulder; the arm stayed on the spike, still lit, and half the Pit saw it glowing on the wall. By the time he could climb the stair-streets the spike was bare but for a dark stain and a strip of black cloth.

The Pit is Eclipsera's old stone quarry, the one the Sprawl cut its stone from, below the Tower District at the foot of Hallowell Tower: now a slum built down its walls for the people the city has no room for. It keeps four tiers: the Floor; the stair-streets that switch back up the walls, the Lane stair and the Shelf stair; the Shelf, a market on a broad ledge halfway up the wall; and the Rim, under the tower's foot. Osgood Tarr, the Pump King, owns the Pit's only clean pumps and sells water by the bucket. His pump chits, called water paper, pass for money in the Pit; his collectors wear his blue on a rag round the arm and take a water toll on goods at the switchbacks, a chit a bag. The Sump, a bar of boards and tin on the Floor, is Tamm Broadhand's (LN7). The stair-streets keep Eclipsera's street register in small: a choirhouse with its bell, the Mendery's door under a hand stitched across the wrist, a rondel court chalked on bare stone, tracts and the Nightglass pasted up, a numbers board, and on the Shelf stair a silent row with tin cups under an old Hallowell billboard. Ruled texture: each congregation works its own pitch and none coordinates; the silent row sits a flight above the Mendery's door, not outside it, and the GC1 metaplot flag is not raised. Nobody in the Pit calls the Constabulary. Book V.3.3.

Tamm Broadhand keeps the Sump. She is an orc of the Tarkesh diaspora whose grandparents came south in the Poisoned River dispersals; her grandfather came out of the Poisoned River one-handed and kept a fish stall in the Pit for forty years, and nobody robbed him twice. She fights with her left hand in her apron pocket and teaches Short Hand (LN9). Dob is a kid who climbs the Pit's walls for scrap and keeps pigeons on the Sump's roof, which he sells to Tamm's kitchen; their hay broke Ilyas's fall. Tamm closed his shoulder with a skillet off the stove, Dob helped her get him inside, and nobody called the Constabulary. Nim Dry-Cup keeps the Sump's pumps running and a pump-parts stall on the Shelf. She is a goblin from the Confederacy duneworks, her taken name is the cup her settlement was never offered, and she knows exactly what his gilt means.

Every named figure of the night is an elf and every crew human, except the goblins and their keeper. Qadir Mell ran the Lantern Bistro for Hallowell: Ilyas's oldest friend, who drank from the family's cup in the same year and kept the family's stop under the Lantern for decades, until Hallowell bought him. He carried Last Orders, a coral-inlaid greataxe, and fell in the street outside his own front door. Brask and Iyla were his second and his knife, Brask with Reservation, a winged spear with a lavender ribbon, and Iyla with Corkscrew, a wavy dagger. Orrin, Hesk and Odile were the Lantern's head chef, sous-chef and quickest knife, with Butcher's Bill, Cold Cut and Eighty-Six. Sable headed Hallowell Tower's lobby security over three human guards and carried Clearance, a silver-hilted longsword. Kade was Hallowell's head of security and carried Severance, a black longsword with a crimson inlay and hawk-wing quillons. Ixet, a lizard-folk exile from the Mountain Sultanate, kept the Line goblins at the Deep Station and fought with a cleaver-glaive and his tail. The goblins are a feral band trapped in the Northern Continuum's shallows and sold south, nested now in the disused tunnels of the Sareth line: a population and not the species (TR2). The six hired men came from the Sprawl's farm edge. The riders came off a Kindling pit-fight circuit, armed from Hallowell's dumped stock, and never broke off as their numbers fell, which is the Kindling's mark. The checkpoint was the Eclipsera Constabulary of the Tower District, on Hallowell's payroll.

Short Hand is a one-handed knife style. Caliphate soldiers who lost hands and arms in the War of the Poisoned River (A.V. 1950 to 1983) came south in the dispersals with no trade but fighting, and built a style out of what they had left. The Tarkesh veterans gave it its name: short a hand, and short with the knife. Its stance is low, the weight forward, the knife tight to the chest, the steps short and chopping and never crossed. The empty side is used, not hidden. In the Hinge it turns into a blow and takes it glancing on the shoulder, and the knife ends inside the man's reach; the Wrist toll cuts the hand that reaches; the Short ladder is a rising stab from the low stance, under the guard; the Blind-side check drives the empty shoulder into a man who is not set; and the Ankle hook puts a foot behind his ankle while the knife threatens high. Its doctrine: your feet are your other hand. Tamm Broadhand learned it on the back step of her grandfather's fish stall. Book VII.5.

Three further styles from the build. The Wire drill is Noon Company's drill on the Confederacy's border wire in the 2270s, a line held across open sand to keep the wells: the blade out on the line between the Ranger and the man, the feet wide and low, every cut thrown whole from the shoulder and carried through, and the finish held a beat before the blade comes back onto the line. It was drilled for a gilded body and does not work without the gilt. Its master stroke, the Long count, is a lunge the gilt carries across the sand. Its doctrine: hold the line; the wire does not go to the man, he comes to it. The Sareth cut is thirty years of Eclipsera enforcement worn into one man's habits: short windups, a small follow-through, a quick return to a tight guard, and a glance round the room after every kill. Its doctrine: do the job, and nothing past it. The Order drill is the baton course every licensed guard in Eclipsera has sat: the Eclipsera Constabulary's public-order course, cut to forty hours and sold to the city's security firms, with the hand-to-hand of Crown Territorial Levy basic bolted on by the old Levies who teach it. Generic, not elite: formally trained civilians. The guard stands upright and side-on, a steel expandable baton at the shoulder and the free hand up in front, palm out, which the course calls the fence. Blows go to the arms and the legs, and the head is a last resort. Partners in reach cover each other, and a man whose partners are down is out of the book. The course ends at the baton push and the arm bar, and nobody masters it. Its doctrine: keep the gap, keep your partner, and go home. Hallowell Tower's lobby guards fought in it on the Long Night once their guns ran dry. Book VII.5.

PROVISIONAL: the rest of Act I, from the author's synopsis, filed as proposed [P] until the build carries it. The scrap arm: Nim Dry-Cup builds Ilyas an arm that holds no charge, because the null kills any cell wired in near him: tension cables, springs, a ratchet hand, and drive gears pulled from recalled Hallowell Doorbell turrets dumped in the Pit (compare the Unstrung, VII.4.5). It grips, braces, throws and hits like a hammer; it cannot hold a blade with any finesse, it jams, and it has to be wound. The Pump King's prize: on the night of the fall Tarr's men pried the lit arm off the spike, and it goes on sale in the Pit as the only intact Noon lattice anyone can buy; Ilyas goes through Tarr's collectors on the stair-streets and his crew in the pumphouse, and takes it back. The joining: Nim bridges the lit lattice in the arm to the dark lattice in the shoulder with gold wire drawn from the arc-blade's gilded edges, and before she closes it the digger and the landholder drink first, together, from one cup: Nim and Ilyas share water from Tarr's own pump, the oath the Charter broke. The arm's light runs across the join and relights him line by line, though the old burned-out lines stay dark; his speed and his workings come back, and the arc-blade locks again. The scrap arm goes up on the wall over the Sump's bar, and Act II begins with the man in white.
